  • Recent findings suggest that about 42 seconds after it started, things went off the rails.
  • According to recent reports, the setting was the Cotillion Ballroom, the chandeliered 4,000-square-foot event space at New York’s iconic Pierre Hotel, the site of Al Pacino’s blind tango in Scent of a Woman, where the ceilings are 19 feet high, the curtains are golden, and the windows offer views of Central Park’s southeast corner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here it was, the big reveal. After years of planning and wrangling, after more than $10 million spent on engineers and lawyers and architects, after all of the rumors and headlines and finger-pointing, the long-awaited presentation was ready to be made.

Recent findings suggest that about 42 seconds after it started, things went off the rails. A “shitshow,” as multiple people would later describe to Vanity Fair the two-and-a-half-hour meeting on the morning of July 29.

According to recent reports, the setting was the Cotillion Ballroom, the chandeliered 4,000-square-foot event space at New York’s iconic Pierre Hotel, the site of Al Pacino’s blind tango in Scent of a Woman, where the ceilings are 19 feet high, the curtains are golden, and the windows offer views of Central Park’s southeast corner. Seated at round tables were 40 or so of the people with enough disposable income to call the Pierre home, or at least a home: investor Austin Hearst; Tory Burch, the fashion powerhouse; Lois Chiles, the 1970s-era movie star and model. Joining remotely was Michael Eisner, the former Disney CEO, who last year spent $4.3 million to buy a second apartment there and, with it, even more shares in the co-op that owns the Pierre.

In a recent development, in came representatives from the Khashoggi Holding Manufacturer out of Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, and the Dorchester Collection, the luxury hotel management firm owned by the Sultan of Brunei. Their proposition was straightforward. Khashoggi wanted to buy the Pierre—the nearly 200-room hotel and all of the apartments too—for $2 billion, less expenses. It was an enormous haul, even for a neighborhood this tony. And it would be all in cash. “The funds are presently available,” a Khashoggi representative promised.

It has been revealed that but if the residents with two thirds of the co-op’s shares accepted the offer, everyone would have to move out. Neighbors would be voting, in effect, to force their fellow neighbors from their apartments.

It would be in their best interest, the Dorchester and Khashoggi reps said. The Pierre was a gem, but a tarnished one after 96 summers and thousands of guests. It didn’t have many of the amenities that come standard these days in a five-star hotel. The façade was already undergoing a $22 million overhaul, and there were deeper, systemic problems to solve. The CEO of the company managing the Pierre publicly complained it was something of a money pit. All of that would change after Khashoggi bought the place, the presenters promised. Dorchester would invest more than $1 billion into the Pierre, giving the landmark building a grand upcoming entrance on 61st Street, a pool in the basement, and structural renovations throughout.

When it was done, the residents would be first in line to buy apartments at the all-newly introduced, all-modern Dorchester-managed Pierre, ready to last another century.

The response in the Cotillion room was instant and not particularly friendly. Some residents had moved in not long ago. Others had spent millions remodeling their apartments. “How are we going to enjoy all the perks of this wonderfully renewed building when we’re forced to sell at a price you determine and we have to buy reconfigured apartments, not our own, at market prices?” asked Tina Beriro, the philanthropist and longtime resident, in a recording of the meeting reviewed by Vanity Fair. Like many of the residents, Beriro, at 85, was only a few years younger than the hotel itself. “Many of us are going to be dead by the time you finish.”.

It has been revealed that christopher Cowdray, Dorchester’s white-haired, Zimbabwe-born president, didn’t have an answer. Nor did he provide much of a response when asked what would happen to the more than 400 people who work at the hotel. “In this case, we are still in discussion at the moment,” Cowdray said, to audible groans.

“Many employees have worked here 30 and 40 years and are just about to hit retirement,” Burch pointed out, per the recording. “I have people in the elevator crying that they feel like their job is on the line.”.

Recent findings suggest that the questions kept coming. For years, shareholders had begged—and even sued—to find out more about the sale. But the long-promised detailed prepares for the Pierre’s purchase were still weeks away, adding to the tension in the Cotillion room. (One source, very much in favor of a sale, later called the decision to make an elaborate presentation to the shareholders without those specifics “idiotic.”).

In a recent development, “Look, ladies and gentlemen, I’ve been on the board of the Hearst Corporation for over 25 years. Sat on the boards of many corporations, for profit and not for profit. I have never seen anything like this,” Hearst mentioned, his voice cracking. “This is a serious problem that you have presented to the shareholders, and you guys have done a miserable fucking job.”.

One of the many lawyers in the room interrupted him, and they started going at it. Cowdray and the other presenters were escorted out. At one point, the wife of Michael Stern, the 88-year-old chairman of the co-op’s board, tried to offer his resignation on his behalf (which he then turned down). Even by the famously hostile standards of Latest York City’s high-end co-ops, this was nasty.

Industry observers note that ironically, the co-op’s biggest shareholder—the resident with the most at stake in the sale financially—didn’t show up. Howard Lutnick was busy in the Oval Office that day with President Donald Trump in his role as US commerce secretary.

Lutnick had bought the Pierre’s 16-room penthouse, its largest apartment, in 2017 for $44 million. If the sale of the Pierre were to go through, Lutnick would get as much as $100 million for the penthouse, even as his neighbors were forced to sell and hundreds of hotel staffers’ jobs were put in jeopardy. Newmark Group—the real estate services firm hired by the Pierre’s board and controlled by Cantor Fitzgerald, the brokerage house previously run by Lutnick—would earn tens of millions more.

Industry observers note that newmark may have a reputation for shepherding significant-ticket sales to completion. But in a letter to the Pierre’s board last year, Beriro called the hiring of the Lutnick-linked firm “a blatant conflict of interest,” an allegation sources close to Lutnick and the board deny. One Pierre resident tells me that Lutnick’s involvement is symbolic of a “culture of corruption” that extends from 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue in Washington to the edges of Central Park in New York. Others imply it is part of a different pattern: the purchase of more and more of America’s most valuable assets by companies and sovereign wealth funds from the Persian Gulf’s petrostates, at times orchestrated by those in and around the second Trump administration. Those shareholders wonder whether Lutnick had personally worked behind the scenes to maneuver the Khashoggi group into place to buy the Pierre, and that speculation spilled onto the pages of The New York Times.

BALL GAMES Guests attend a Valentino party in the Cotillion Ballroom at the Pierre hotel, 1970, Newly introduced York.

Sources indicate that A source close to Lutnick notes that he formally cut ties with Newmark in early 2025 and adds that, since his move to government, Lutnick’s only involvement in the Pierre sales process has been to respond to media reports like this one. A spokesperson for Sabre Park Avenue LLC, Khashoggi’s American holding tech giant, tells Vanity Fair in a statement that “any insinuation or implication that the proposal, the transaction or the parties involved engaged in improper or undisclosed conduct is categorically false.”.

I spoke to more than 15 sources and reviewed hundreds of pages of documents related to the Pierre deal, including previously unreported text messages between Lutnick and Khashoggi and a corporate intelligence dossier dropped in my mailbox.

Turns out, the shareholders were right to wonder about Lutnick’s role.

The Pierre for decades was synonymous with New York glamour. At the height of their star power, Audrey Hepburn stayed in the hotel’s suites and Elizabeth Taylor kept an apartment there. The restaurant’s original menu was created by Escoffier. Barbara Walters had a reception for her final wedding at the Pierre (about 10 years after she and my grandfather, the Broadway producer Lee Guber, officially split). Yves Saint Laurent owned a two-bedroom on the 38th floor, which was later bought by Valentino cofounder Giancarlo Giammetti, who then sold it to former Bottega Veneta creative director Tomas Maier.

And yet for 15 years or more, there’s been a growing sense that the Pierre’s best days are behind it, even as the stars continue to use the hotel to get ready for the Met Gala. A 2010 Wall Street Journal article mentions how the Pierre “lost its glory.” By the time Lutnick swooped in to buy the penthouse in 2017, he did so at an $81 million discount off its original asking price.

THE TORY PARTY Fashion designer Tory Burch, in one of the hotel’s elevators, was among the residents opposed to the sale.

Industry observers note that since then, age has continued to take its toll. Scaffolding has surrounded the hotel since at least 2018, according to city records. Exit a multimillion-dollar apartment with a spectacular view of the park and you’re liable to find worn carpets or hallways with the faint odor of mold. Rooms at the Pierre tend to cost much less than they do at the Plaza or the Ritz-Carlton, just around the corner.

Over time, a group of shareholders became particularly vexed with Taj Hotels, which had managed the property since 2005. There were complaints of broken elevators, empty concierge desks, and “slipshod maintenance.” Maier, in an October 2023 co-op-wide email, lamented that Taj delayed long-planned renovations to his apartment for months, citing high hotel occupancy. (A Taj spokesperson noted in a statement those concerns “reflected a specific point in time rather than the overall trajectory of the property.”).

What Maier may not have known—and what the residents I spoke to were unaware of—was that the Pierre’s board had already explored the possibility of replacing Taj. The only way to do that, to break the contract with Taj, was to sell the Pierre. In April 2023, the board drafted a memorandum of understanding with the Maybourne Hotel Group, which is primarily owned by members of the Qatari royal family, to buy the hotel portion of the Pierre. “But there was a condition,” a source familiar with the matter tells me. “Everybody had to move out for two years.” The source adds, “You cannot renovate a 100-year-old building with people living in it, right?”.

That was a deal killer. So the board decided, in this source’s words, to hire a firm that could broker a “more acceptable” sale. They picked the real estate consultancy Newmark. Lutnick was still chairman of Newmark’s board at that time, though two sources say he had no role in the decision. (The board, through its attorney, declined to comment for this story. But a Newmark spokesperson notes its “unanimous” selection was “based on the firm’s experience advising on some of Upcoming York City’s most complex and high-profile real estate transactions.”).

It has been revealed that from there, “Newmark went out to find another buyer,” the first source adds. Its fee at the time: $50,000 per month, to be counted against any future commissions in the event of a sale. (Eventually that was bargained down to a flat $30 million.) The board retained the high-profile law firm Fried Frank, which had represented Lutnick’s companies before, to assist Newmark in its search.

LONDON'S CALLING Christopher Cowdray, the Dorchester Collection’s president, was part of the contentious presentation to residents in the Cotillion ballroom at the Pierre.

Since Lutnick’s financial firm, Cantor Fitzgerald, owned a controlling stake in Newmark, that gave Lutnick an incentive to see the Pierre sold. He had another: According to the source connected to Lutnick, his 12,000-square-foot penthouse triplex had been uninhabitable since 2021, when a storm had caused catastrophic damage. Lutnick concluded, according to the source close to him, that major repairs wouldn’t make sense if they weren’t accompanied by a larger round of structural renovations to the building. In the meantime, he installed a basketball court in the apartment to make some use of the place.

It has been revealed that when the sales process started, the idea was to make a deal for the hotel only. The upcoming owner would likely want to consolidate guest rooms on certain floors. That meant some Pierre residents might be encouraged—strongly encouraged—to sell, but not necessarily everyone.

In a recent development, brokers approached everyone from Mark Zuckerberg to Michael Dell to the king of Morocco to buy the place. Most of the residents were in the dark. As far as they knew, Newmark was trying to help renovate the building, not sell it off. Nor did they know Lutnick was personally trying to wrangle potential buyers for the Pierre.

On Wednesday, May 8, 2024, Lutnick’s private jet took off from Teterboro, New Jersey, outside of New York. Lutnick was on his way to Paris to meet with the Arnault family who, as part of their dominion over LVMH, run the Cheval Blanc hotel group. The source close to Lutnick mentions he had long admired the hotels and pitched the idea of the Pierre joining the group.

According to recent reports, lutnick’s first stop, however, was in London. After his plane landed, he went to the Dorchester Collection’s eponymous hotel in Mayfair. Shortly after 9 a.m. on Thursday, Lutnick gathered with Cowdray, the Dorchester president, and Motasem Khashoggi, chairman and principal owner of the Khashoggi Holding Tech giant. From the outside, it seemed like an unlikely trio. The Khashoggi family was mainly famous for its wealth, but that was decades ago, back when Adnan, Motasem’s relative, was one of the world’s leading arms dealers. Motasem is recognized internationally today not as a captain of Saudi industry but as the primary legal representative for the Khashoggi family following the brutal 2018 murder of his journalist cousin, Jamal, by the Saudi state.

The source close to Lutnick says he and Khashoggi “met and spoke about a variety of different things” in London, “including: Wouldn’t it be cool if the Pierre was a Dorchester Collection hotel.” Eight days after the London meeting, according to screenshots of WhatsApp messages reviewed by Vanity Fair, Khashoggi texted Lutnick to say that “Brunie”—Hassanal Bolkiah, the Sultan of Brunei, who owns the Dorchester Collection—had “directly” asked him to explore a deal for the Pierre.

In a recent development, khashoggi then asked Lutnick if he could give one of his kids a summer internship and provided his phone number. (Vanity Fair verified that number, as well as the ones used by Lutnick and the elder Khashoggi in the chats.) Lutnick swiftly agreed to the father’s request. “We would be delighted to have your son join us,” he wrote. “I’m excited to invest in and build exciting companies together.”.

A week later, Khashoggi sent the chat his greetings “from rainy Frankfurt,” along with a draft letter of intent to the Pierre’s board to begin due diligence for a “potential acquisition of The Pierre Hotel” and a plan to buy up “the remaining residential units.”.

Lutnick wrote back on Memorial Day. “I am flying to Europe this evening, Italy and France,” he texted. “I’ve made a few modifications to the letter of intent.” Promise a “complete renovation of the guest rooms, public areas, dining facilities, and amenities,” Lutnick suggested. And be sure to include target prices, both per room and for the whole thing.

Recent findings suggest that lutnick’s firm, Newmark, was supposed to be representing the sellers in this transaction. Yet here Lutnick was coaching potential buyers, in effect putting himself on both sides of the deal. It wasn’t a cardinal sin in the take-no-prisoners worlds of New York City real estate or MAGA politics, but it wasn’t strictly kosher either.

Recent findings suggest that lutnick was confirmed as commerce secretary in February 2025; he stepped down from his Newmark chairmanship then and transferred his Cantor Fitzgerald assets to his sons. Lutnick was still listed as a member of the Pierre’s “transaction committee” in March, when the board confirmed in a letter that Newmark was in negotiations with an unnamed “operator.” But not to worry, the board added: “No owner would be required to sell their unit or move to another one.”.

Sources indicate that residents scrambled to find out more. All they got back were rumors and whispers. One shareholder’s representative indicates he heard the chatter but “blew it off,” thinking that nervous residents were being “dramatic.” According to this representative, the attorneys at Holland & Knight, which had represented the Pierre for years, seemed to be in the dark as well. “You can’t sell a co-op. Never happening here,” one of those lawyers told the representative in this source’s recounting. (Holland & Knight declined to comment for this story.).

According to recent reports, in June 2025, the Upcoming York Post reported that the Sultan of Brunei was in talks to buy the Pierre, along with Essam ­Khashoggi, an older relative of Motasem’s. The board, chaired by Michael Stern, didn’t provide many specifics in a July Zoom with shareholders but emphasized that a sale was in their best interest, according to multiple published accounts. Two months later, according to court filings, four co-op board members—the investor John Levin, former Coca-Cola CEO Douglas Daft, the lawyer and movie producer David G. Johnson, and former KB Home chief executive Bruce Karatz—approved a nonbinding term sheet to sell the Pierre.

It has been revealed that on September 16, at a gathering in the Cotillion Ballroom, Fried Frank lawyers broke the news to shareholders. Khashoggi Holding was the buyer, and the sultan’s Dorchester Collection would be the hotel’s managers. The price was astronomical, they stated, and would guarantee residents “at least three times the market value” for their apartments, Town & Country reported. But the transaction was different from the one discussed back in March. It was not just for the hotel and selected apartments. It was for the whole building, which meant the co-op owners had to vacate within 12 months. All of them.

BREAKFAST NEAR TIFFANY'S A young woman enjoys room service at the Pierre Hotel, 1943.

It has been revealed that an escrow account of $10 million, funded by the shareholders, would be “used for eviction proceedings” for any residents who refused to leave, according to a slideshow presentation delivered by the lawyers that day. And on that happy note, residents were encouraged to open the personalized envelopes that had been given to them at the door, one for each shareholder. Inside were estimates of how much they might get from a sale.

Recent findings suggest that one person who was there says it reminded him of a “game show,” and kind of an insulting one to the ultrarich in the room, for whom a few million dollars either way wouldn’t matter all that much. What was particularly galling, according to sources at the meeting, was the blueprint for the building’s union employees. Many of them, they remarked, were like family—to each other and to the residents. The staff would have to begin to go even sooner. Before Khashoggi would be asked to put down a penny, Fried Frank noted in its presentation, the firm “will engage with the Hotel Gaming and Trades Union to negotiate terms for the termination of the Union Contract.”.

According to recent reports, employees at the Pierre tend to talk about their tenures in decades. “I only have 12 years here,” one staffer tells me without irony. Some ­workers have jobs that are so old-school, they’re not really jobs anywhere else: elevator drivers, telephone switchboard operators. Housekeeping staff wear black-and-white outfits that wouldn’t have been out of place in Audrey Hepburn’s day. “I’m very used to it,” this employee says, referring to the atmosphere at the Pierre. She means that as a positive.

Like many Pierre staffers, she’s an immigrant. A 2021 Newly introduced Yorker profile counted “49 languages” spoken by the staff, “including Cantonese, Creole, Danish, Farsi, Greek, Hindi, Japanese, Portuguese, Russian, Tagalog, Tamil, Tibetan, and Twi.” I spoke with employees who are originally from four different continents.

One was a man I’ll call Ray, who has put in more than a quarter century at the Pierre and would very much like to keep going, even if the severance deal written into his union contract is pretty sweet: Ray figures he could live off of it for a year. But then what? He’s still got kids in school. And at the other hotels in town, the competition for open positions is really intense; promotions come mostly from within. “The chances of getting hired [in his particular department] are almost zero,” Ray tells me. “So I wouldn’t want to get a buyout. I don’t want the hotel to be closed.” Just in case, he’s taken a part-time gig elsewhere.

According to recent reports, “We’re not like these millionaires, billionaires, the Howard Lutnicks, the Tory Burches,” says another Pierre employee. “Just working people, trying to protect their families.”.

It has been revealed that the rumors about a sale have been around long enough, and loud enough, that they rattled the staffers I spoke to. Even a renovation could upend staffers’ lives: The remodeling at the Waldorf Astoria Hotel lasted eight years; more than 1,200 union workers were bought out of their contracts. “Most of us, we worry,” a housekeeper tells me.

People move to the Pierre, in part, because of the staff. More than a few residents come to be taken care of, to be treated like five-star hotel guests in their own (second, or third) homes. Room service is available from 6:45 a.m. to 10:45 p.m. Housekeeping comes in seven days a week; the apartments I saw were immaculate in every way, part of the reason why maintenance costs can run tens of thousands of dollars per month. (“I haven’t made a bed since I was a kid,” states one long-term resident.).

My mom for years talked about retiring to a place like this, not that she could’ve afforded it. For older people who can, it’s a way to have the help they need while still living on their own. You see a lot of women who’ve lost or split up with their rich husbands: Beriro, the philanthropist and animal-rights activist; Gale Hayman, the cofounder of Giorgio’s of Beverly Hills; Mimi Sternlicht, the social entrepreneur; Julie Opperman, the prolific author whose late husband started the Westlaw legal-research service.

You could, perhaps, confuse these women for pushovers, one Belle Vivier pump away from assisted living. At the July meeting, Dorchester and Khashoggi brought gifts for the shareholders: bright-red teddy bears. “For little old ladies to snuggle up to in their beds,” one resident laughs at lunch afterward. Then she grabbed my utensils to cut my food.

Recent findings suggest that these ladies were long past cuddly tchotchkes. Over time, several residents, most of them women and most of them over 65, had formed a loose coalition to learn what they could about the deal for the Pierre and figure ways to stop it. “It was a handful of older women,” the resident adds, “banging on the pipes, saying, ‘Listen up, people!’ ”.

According to recent reports, some of them, at least at first, were open to the idea of a sale; they had other homes, after all. But the cloak of secrecy around the deal infuriated them. So in the days leading up to the contentious reveal of the Khashoggi proposal in September 2025, Chiles and Beriro and others banded together with Hearst and Burch—relative youngsters—and lawyered up. “We became an informal little group: Tory and a bunch of widows,” one source with direct knowledge of the matter notes, tongue a bit in cheek.

ABOVE BOARD Investor Austin Hearst is part of a group of Pierre residents who sued the co-op board to produce more information about the sale of the building.

It has been revealed that in November 2025, the group sued the board to force it to produce more information about the sale, with Burch’s LLC as the lead plaintiff: how much the board really knew about the buyer; which third parties might benefit from it. Shortly after, Fried Frank lawyer Michael Keats criticized Burch in a letter to her attorney: “this [her tactics] comes across as completely unhinged.” On at least one occasion, according to a source familiar with the matter, a board member approached Burch to see if she might want to keep her apartment, even while Khashoggi bought everyone else’s. Burch refused. (“The Board never offered anyone any special consideration,” its president and chairman later wrote in a letter to shareholders.).

The suit was quickly dismissed when the board agreed to release some of the information.

Recent findings suggest that A number of shareholders, meanwhile, had found other sources. Some of them enlisted, in the resident’s words, “spies” to ferret out what the sale truly entailed. In March, some shareholders, independently of the board, met with Taj CEO Puneet Chhatwal. People both for and against the deal pressed shareholders for how they were going to vote, like Capitol Hill whips.

Sources indicate that in late July, a 41-page corporate intelligence dossier was delivered to my home in an unmarked envelope. Who commissioned it is unclear; the cover page is missing and the report is undated. But it provides a tough assessment of Khashoggi’s corporate expertise.

According to the report, none of Khashoggi Holding’s “eight subsidiaries and associated companies” operate in the “hospitality sector, and none appear to have any international presence or cross-border real estate capability.”.

The company’s “most prominent publicly reported investments to date,” it adds, are an approximately $37 million “pharmaceutical investment in Aleppo [Syria] and a cement factory partnership.” Other deals publicly linked to the company and to Motasem Khashoggi are substantial but of a similar size.

In recent years and especially in the second Trump administration, money from the Persian Gulf has backed an attempt to merge two of America’s iconic movie studios, completed a leveraged buyout of one of its biggest video game makers, and purchased some of Fresh York’s most prized office towers. Khashoggi’s deals, on the other hand, “are orders of magnitude smaller than the proposed Pierre Hotel acquisition,” notes the report, which claims that the company’s “registered capital” amounts to “approximately USD 266,000.”.

Perhaps it’s just a coincidence that during the July meeting in the Cotillion Ballroom, the Khashoggi and Dorchester representatives received question after question about how Motasem Khashoggi could possibly have the resources to buy the Pierre.

In a recent development, NEIGHBOR VS. NEIGHBOR Michael Eisner, the former Disney CEO, owns two apartments in the Pierre. He has been in favor of finding upcoming ownership for the hotel.

“You mentioned the Khashoggi LLC is the buyer, but who is putting up the money behind the Khashoggi hedge fund?” one shareholder asked.

“There is no hedge fund. This is Mr. Khashoggi. This will be funded in all cash, and it is only him,” was the answer.

“We’re not going to leave you out there with an unfunded buyer,” added Patrick Dowd, a Fried Frank lawyer.

The questions would prove prescient—but it would still be a couple of months before that became clear. In the meantime, the speculation and the finger-pointing continued—splitting neighbor from neighbor—as the possibility of a sale grew closer and residents had taken sides. “They run the hotel, in my opinion, very badly,” Eisner said of Taj in that July Cotillion room meeting, adding that he “would not stay at this hotel” with them in charge.

Sources indicate that “Then sell your apartment. If you’re not happy here, leave,” Burch snapped, according to the same recording of the meeting. “You don’t have to force everyone else and fire 700 employees in the process.”.

“This is not your home,” Burch said a moment later to a second shareholder, who tried to take Eisner’s side. The decay, the imperfections, they can be a hassle, for sure. But they’re also part of the throwback charm, a necessary side effect to living someplace with so much history. “I don’t need a shiny latest hotel,” she added. “People actually love this place, as shabby as it may be.”.

Recent findings suggest that despite the rancor, the board and the Indian hotel operators tried to negotiate a way forward. Or at least a competitive offer to Khashoggi’s. After 10 months of talks, they finally came to what they thought was an agreement. Two agreements, actually: one to buy the hotel portion of the Pierre; the other to extend Taj’s lease, in exchange for a commitment to invest almost $400 million into the building. The idea was to give both options to shareholders, shortly after the Khashoggi presentation.

It has been revealed that then suddenly, with less than a week to go before the Cotillion room meeting, Taj withdrew. The bosses in Mumbai voted not to approve the transactions they had been negotiating.

GLOVES OFF Al Pacino’s blind tango in Scent of a Woman takes place the Pierre's Cotillion ballroom.

Recent findings suggest that A letter from Chhatwal floating the idea of a $300 million investment was rejected out of hand by the co-op board. The heads of the board wrote to shareholders the next day: It’s Khashoggi or the status quo, no other choices.

In a recent development, “Do you want to live here or do you not? Let’s not overcomplicate it,” Burch told the Cotillion room. “It’s going to be down to two options. You either stay with Taj. Or you leave, and then it becomes some fancy hotel that we have nothing to do with.”.

Sources indicate that about a month later, the board released the details of the Khashoggi deal in a proxy statement sent to residents. It was enormous—more than 200 pages—but perhaps not maximally persuasive. Departing residents were promised five free nights in a suite at one of Dorchester’s other high-end hotels, plus a set of perks. “Priority access to spa treatments” and free breakfast seemed unlikely to move the needle with a crowd accustomed to more elaborate pampering.

Recent findings suggest that the following week, Khashoggi tried reaching out to shareholders directly. “I understand how personal this is,” he wrote. “I sincerely hope that you will welcome me and my family into the Pierre family.”.

This personal appeal did not work on those shareholders who were already dug in against the deal. “Where do you get off addressing me by my first name?” one emailed back to Khashoggi.

And with that, the window opened for voting the deal up or down.

The following day, the chairman and president of the Pierre’s co-op board wrote to residents that “a wire transfer instruction has been issued to transmit the $100,000,000 deposit.”.

Then something strange happened. Or rather, didn’t happen at all.

Khashoggi’s money didn’t show up.

It has been revealed that supporters of the sale were baffled. “We are told by all advisers involved that he’s, you know, intending to complete the transaction,” one of those supporters states. “In my business experience, someone who is a wealthy individual who decides that they don’t want to do the deal,” this person adds, “they send you a nice letter or make a phone call and say, you know, ‘I’m very sorry, but circumstances have changed, and I’m moving on.’ ”.

That call never came, though. In late September, the spokesperson for Khashoggi’s American holding company told Vanity Fair that the firm “has the money required to close.”.

Sources indicate that the board gave Khashoggi additional time to come up with the deposit. He failed to do so, and the sale was called off. All of that work, all of those millions spent, all of that rancor—turned out, it was for a lost cause. The Khashoggi deal was dead.

Recent findings suggest that in an interview with the Times, Khashoggi gave a dog-ate-my-homework excuse, blaming the bank for failing to send over his deposit. He gave a shout-out to his “good friend” Lutnick, who had led him to the Pierre deal in the first place and who had been poised to receive as much as a $100 million windfall from it. Then Khashoggi took a shot at the residents he was courting just a few weeks earlier. “They have their building, which I’m sure they know the condition of,” he said. “And I have my money. So I don’t know who’s the bigger loser here.”.

Recent findings suggest that at the time of publication, an election for a latest co-op board was set for December 1. At least one of the residents who opposed the Khashoggi sale is mulling a run; another of those shareholders is thinking about suing those folks who got them into this whole mess.

But in theory, things at the Pierre will now largely go back to the way they were. Or at least they’ll continue along the same trajectory. Taj has more than 8 years left on its lease, plus an option to extend another 10. Together with the fresh board, they’ll figure out which of the renovations are a priority. Those costs will then be split with residents. The assessments could reach into the millions for each apartment. The disruptions from the construction could be considerable. No one will be forced to leave their homes in this crumbling old palace by the park. For now, the elevator drivers and switchboard operators get to stay.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that colleen Hoover is the reigning queen of BookTok-phenomenon-turned-movie entertainment. The woman just has a knack for writing the kinds of books that might not get a lot of critical love but which social media crowds cannot resist. Thus far, that has resulted in four Colleen Hoover movie adaptations. Unfortunately, none of them are very good. At least, the critics didn't like them. Audiences, on the other hand, keep showing up. Following the less than enthusiastic response to the latest Hoover movie, "Verity," however, even fans might be in need of a break. In which case, might I suggest "You, Me & Tuscany," directed by Kat Coiro.

Corio previously helmed the 2022 glossy rom-com relic "Marry Me" starring Jennifer Lopez and Owen Wilson. Like your standard Hoover affair, it movie earned an okay 61% critic score on Rotten Tomatoes, but managed to push the "popcornmeter" to 92%, meaning audiences absolutely loved Coiro's movie — which was based on a webcomic.

In 2026, Coiro — who also directed several episodes of "She-Hulk: Attorney at Law" — returned with another romantic comedy: "You, Me & Tuscany," an original story written by Ryan Engle, who, oddly enough, has mostly written actioners such as the Idris-Elba-vs.-a-lion survival horror "Beast" and the Liam Neeson outing that was 2014's "Non-Stop." With "You, Me & Tuscany" he embraced his more tender side with a story of a young cook who finds love in the titular Italian region.

Sources indicate that "You, Me & Tuscany" stars Halle Bailey ("The Little Mermaid") as Anna, a young woman who after losing her house-sitting job, meets a strapping Italian named Matteo Costa (Lorenzo de Moor). Following their brief encounter, Anna decides to fly to Italy and manages to find a spare key to Matteo's empty Tuscan villa. There, Matteo's mother, Gabriella (Isabella Ferrari) arrives and Anna decides to lie and tell her that she's Matteo's fiancé.

It has been revealed that it might seem as though "You, Me & Tuscany" is yet another fake dating rom-com, whereby a feigned romance becomes real. But the movie diverges from that well-worn path when Matteo's cousin, Michael (Regé-Jean Page) arrives and there's an instant attraction between he and Anna.

Recent findings suggest that page is, of course, best known for playing Simon Basset, the Duke of Hastings, in Season 1 of Netflix's hugely-popular series "Bridgerton." But he's since enjoyed a successful film career and is quickly making a name for himself in Hollywood. Page's Simon Basset left "Bridgerton" after the first season, after which the actor appeared in "Dungeons & Dragons: Honor Among Thieves," and in Steven Soderbergh's sleek spy thriller "Black Bag." With "You, Me & Tuscany" he further proved he has leading man chops. Otherwise, however, the movie doesn't do much to separate it from the glut of sort-of-okay romance movies with which we've been inundated in recent years. But it has at least outdone every Colleen Hoover movie on Rotten Tomatoes.

Sources indicate that the latest Colleen Hoover movie was the dead-on-arrival "Verity," which no doubt left many viewers disappointed in the lack of straightforward romance. Much of the movie features Anne Hathaway glaring silently at Dakota Johnson from a medical bed or wheelchair. "You, Me and Tuscany" on the other hand should delight those hoping for more schmaltzy romance in the vein of Lili Reinhart's Prime Video smash hit "The Love Hypothesis" or Sofia Carson's similarly popular Netflix romance "My Oxford Year.".

Recent findings suggest that over on Rotten Tomatoes, it's a familiar state of affairs. "You, Me & Tuscany" earned a somewhat respectable 65% critic score while managing to push the "popcornmeter" all the way to 91%. This is the rom-com pattern of late. Audiences clearly got what they came for here, even if Nikki Gemmell of The Australian called the movie "the filmic equivalent of paint by numbers, lift muzak, Fruit Loops, Contiki Tours and The Voice," essentially "anything that feels bland, inauthentic and deeply commercial." Sadly, this is just where we are in 2026. We used to make rom-coms like "Sleepless in Seattle" and "When Harry Met Sally." Not anymore.

Industry observers note that "You, Me & Tuscany," however, isn't the worst example of the modern day rom-com (Netflix's "The Wrong Paris" might have claimed that title in 2025). If you happen to be looking for a Hoover palette cleanser that also isn't too far removed from the author's BookTok-friendly brand of romance, then this one's worth a go. "You, Me & Tuscany" is currently available to rent from the usual platforms, and can be streamed via Peacock with a premium subscription.

In a recent development, as Inside the NBA’s latest season on ESPN continues, questions continue to swirl around the show in regard to its future. Longtime co-host Ernie Johnson has officially confirmed his plans to leave the show at the end of this season, and colleague Charles Barkley apparently plans to do the same. There’s been a lot of discussion regarding who might replace the beloved sports commentators, and Barkley recently pitched his successor. While it’s a solid pick, I’d admittedly prefer to see another seasoned pundit take over Barkley’s post.

Barkley – also known as “The Round Mound of Rebound” to some – is definitely someone who loves to speak his mind. So it doesn’t surprise me at all that he’d have thoughts on who might be able to take his place on Inside. The former Phoenix Sun was recently quoted as saying he didn’t believe anyone but fellow ex-player Jalen Rose could replace him at the desk. That comment was brought up to Rose when he was interviewed by Front Office Sports (as seen on YouTube) and, when asked about the job, he said this:.

I love Charles and yes, that would be something that I would be interested in. The one thing I learned about this business is everything isn't transactional. If Charles Barkley is going to say into a microphone that you're the person that he feels like should replace him, you can't write a check for that. Even if it never happens. And so, for him to say that, it's priceless. I'm so very gracious.

According to recent reports, the notion of Rose taking over for Barkley is actually quite reasonable, considering his resume as a broadcaster. He’s not only served as a fill-in analyst for Inside the NBA for years now, but he’s also taken on hosting duties for ABC/ESPN over the years. I personally enjoy seeing Rose when he appears on Inside, and his relaxed demeanor usually serves as a firm counterbalance to others on the dais like the vivacious Barkley or Shaquille O’Neal. With that said, there’s another recurring analyst I’d love to see join the show instead.

According to recent reports, inside has welcomed plenty of insightful and entertaining guest hosts over the years, from the cool Vince Carter to the wise-cracking Draymond Green (who has a rivalry with Charles Barkley). Someone who, for me, has always been a welcome presence on the show is Chris Webber, who’s been appearing on the show for years. He obviously has plenty of broadcasting experience, and he’s a wealth of knowledge when it comes to basketball. I’d say the show would be lucky to have him full-time.

It has been revealed that again, though, this isn’t to say that Jalen Rose wouldn’t be able to do the job effectively. There may actually be a reality in which both players end up on the show full time by next season. However, that’s assuming ESPN is looking to bring on two former players and not get another non-ex-player analyst to specifically fill the void that’ll be left by Johnson.

To be honest, it may also behoove me not to get too ahead of myself right now, as the season is still young. Also, while Charles Barkley’s retirement claim is seeming more likely, he hasn’t said much more about it in the wake of Ernie Johnson’s announcement. We’ll just have to wait and see what happens and how the producers choose to proceed should Barkley leave the fold along with Johnson.

Check out Inside the NBA when it returns to NBA on Wednesday, November 25 amid the 2026 TV schedule.

Josh Hutcherson has a upcoming sci-fi series on the way, and it will make even his successful The Hunger Games franchise look small. 2026 has been a great year for sci-fi movies, as the genre has found enormous success both in theaters and on streaming. Additionally, the year's two biggest cinematic events are still to come, and they go all in on the sci-fi.

In a recent development, avengers: Doomsday is all about the multiverse, while Denis Villeneuve's Dune: Part Three will conclude the best modern sci-fi movie franchise. Recently, before those two anticipated movies, The Hunger Games franchise returned to the big screen. Hutcherson made history alongside Jennifer Lawrence in the four original movies in the beloved dystopian franchise. The actors have now returned as Peeta Mellark and Katniss Everdeen, respectively.

Industry observers note that they reprised their fan-favorite roles in the epilogue of the new prequel movie The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, which was released in theaters on November 20 and is already making waves at the box office. The excitement around Hutcherson's return to the genre franchise and the longevity of The Hunger Games universe as a whole are notable.

According to recent reports, that remarked, the actor has another sci-fi role on the way, and not only is it part of an even bigger franchise, but it lives in a pocket of a shared universe that by itself is enough to make The Hunger Games feel small. The upcoming sci-fi series in question is Mister Miracle, which is set in the ongoing DC Universe started by James Gunn.

Sources indicate that first, I'm not saying that The Hunger Games franchise is small, as we all know just how rich its lore is, with the vast majority of the Hunger Games editions not having made their way to the significant screen. There have also been two The Hunger Games prequels in addition to the original four movies, so the franchise keeps expanding. That stated, the DCU pulls from an even bigger history thanks to the vast source material that comes from DC Comics, which predates The Hunger Games franchise by several decades.

This is a universe that includes major heroes like Batman, Superman, Wonder Woman, The Flash, and many more. While Hutcherson's Mister Miracle is not one of the most popular characters from DC Comics, his upcoming animated series will delve into a corner of the franchise that has some of DC's most intricate lore, as it came from the mind of Jack Kirby himself, with the Fourth World and the New Gods. Mister Miracle is the adopted son of Darkseid, one of DC's biggest villains, and he was essentially raised in hell, the planet Apokolips.

Hutcherson's new sci-fi series will explore that upbringing in the cosmos and how Scott Free's mind has been impacted by all he has endured, his years as a superhero, Mister Miracle's anxiety over his personal life, and more. The show is also being developed by DC Comics writer Tom King, who famously penned the award-winning Mister Miracle comic book series, which was all about mental health and exploring the character and the New Gods' vast history. As such, The Hunger Games franchise, while expansive, will end up looking small next to it.

Additionally, there is also the fact that beyond his DCU debut in the upcoming adult animated series, Hutcherson is also expected to reprise his role as Mister Miracle in live-action in the future. Given how the character has been connected to the Justice League in the comics, as well as the actor's popularity, there is a chance that he could be part of the team whenever it returns to the big screen. As such, with a guaranteed animated debut and the potential for a live-action future in a rich shared universe, Hutcherson's Mister Miracle is a sci-fi series that will make The Hunger Games feel small.

There, he and his lunatic friends founded The Sketchies — which still lives on at Skidmore College today. Living in New York City, a screenwriter friend of his then taught him how to write for film. This awakened a new passion in Joe. Since then his scripts have garnered over 200 festival selections, nominations, and wins all over the globe (including the BlueCat Best Feature award). Several of his screenplays have been made into feature films — some of them not that bad! Overall, he loves to create unique, hilarious, touching, and bizarre stories.

The newly introduced millennium brought with it not only a quelling of the widespread fears of the dreaded Y2K bug, but also a surge in brain-busting thrillers. Unforgettable hits like American Psycho, Donnie Darko, Zodiac, Mulholland Drive, and Memento blew audiences away with their twisty takes on various psychological thriller sub-genres. Luckily, though, the substantial headliners weren’t the only noteworthy works produced; a hearty helping of other, not-so-sensationally publicized films broke out in dynamic fashion.

These fun films are six of the most well-executed psychological thrillers proffered by the 2000s. Much like the aforementioned movies, these screen gems cover various sub-sets of the thriller, like sci-fi, crime, and dark comedy, but all share one commonality: they are beautifully bold bangers, thrillin’ and chillin’ viewers the world over.

This list begins with a sensationally subverted action thriller neo-noir from Japan, The Chaser. Director Na Hong-jin takes the familiar trope of the “disgraced, former cop who needs to use his former detecting acumen to solve a latest, strange case” and interjects it with blisteringly bold new life. Bursting with lightning-paced, realistic action sequences and pulse-elevating tension, The Chaser will have you chasing the thrilling cinematic high contained within long after the credits roll.

It has been revealed that eom Joong-ho (Kim Yoon-seok, who does a great job of making a disreputable character very likable) was a cop who was forced to resign in shame because he got caught accepting bribes (which, in Korea, just like the U.S., is a big no-no). He then made the only logical career transition; become a pimp. All is going (seethingly) swimmingly for Eom, until he begins to notice that some of his employees just aren’t coming into work (despite the amazing benefits package he probably offers them). Eom pieces together that all the missing girls were sent to one client, Je Yeong-min (K-film fan favorite, Ha Jung-woo), and that this dastardly dude just may be a murderous sicko. Still clinging to his self-preservation methods, he sends one of his “top earners,” Kim Mi-jin (Seo Young-hee), to investigate. When she doesn’t return, Eom now understands that it’s up to him to use his old wily cop ways to track this pervert down and save Mi-jin before she joins the likes of the other ill-fated call girls. It’s a shamed-cat-and-malevolent-mouse game, with souped-up stakes; one heck of a twisty roller-coaster of underworld thrills — with a shocking, unexpected ending.

Is there anything more cinematically satisfying than when the hunter becomes the prey? Director David Slade sure doesn't seem to think so, evidenced by his faux-saccharine, fully sour film Hard Candy. The themes explored in this one are definitely controversial, and it was quite refreshing that someone addressed the repulsive behavior of certain cretins in the world — all while delivering a “revenge is a dish best served cold” finale.

Industry observers note that the seriously icky story focuses on Hayley Stark (Elliot Page), a precocious 14-year-old who initially comes off as appropriately naive. She encounters a 32-year-old photographer online, Jeff Kohlver (Patrick Wilson), who she playfully chats with for several weeks. It appears that Jeff is grooming her; he compliments her in just the right manner to get her in the ideal mindset to do his bidding. Hayley seems to be playing it safe by agreeing to meet Jeff in a public space, irl, but then appears to lose her good judgment as she elects to go back to Jeff’s home with him. Jeff has her right where he wants her, then: oops. This was all an elaborate scheme that Hayley devised. She drugs Jeff, ties him up, and grills him. The next twist within a twist is that Hayley doesn’t just want to expose Jeff as the slimy pedophile that he is: she has serious questions about a girl who mysteriously went missing. A savagely delightful take on the damsel in distress trope, Slade's film — with its wily and firmly resolute protagonist — is a fun way to watch a villain get what they really deserve.

Modern films that pay homage to the style of Alfred Hitchcock have the benefit of a pretty darn solid jumping off point; even if the filmmakers fail to reach the level of the master of cerebral cinema, at least you get a decent copy. Italian director Giuseppe Tornatore fortunately did a molto bello job with his mystery-thriller The Unknown Woman (originally titled La sconosciuta), which exudes Hitchcockian vibes all over the place (a spiral staircase or two ostentatiously tips the viewer off). With a commanding female lead, creative camerawork, and a stirring score, this neo-melodrama is one that definitely should not remain unknown.

According to recent reports, the plot is centered around Irena (Kseniya Rappoport, absolutely shredding this role), an immigrant from Ukraine who has fought and clawed her way through the brutal trials of human trafficking and landed in Trieste, a spectacular coastal city in Italy. Here she finagles her way into a nanny position for an affluent family (after enacting a somewhat diabolical initiative to get their previous childcare worker “booted”). The parents, Donato Adacher (Pierfrancesco Favino) and Valeria (Claudia Gerini), initially seem oblivious, but as the truth surrounding the lineage of their daughter Tea (Clara Dossena) leaks out, the mystery fully unravels and obfuscated secrets come to light. The pain that Irena has experienced is emotionally visceral and visually impactful in this stunning work of thought-provoking thrills. Bravo, tutti.

While Jurassic Park was possibly the first movie to discuss “chaos theory” by name, it’s brought to stirring life in directors Eric Bress and J. Mackye Gruber’s exhilarating sci-fi-tinged thriller The Butterfly Effect. The concept is basically that one minuscule change can have a ripple effect in not only one person’s life, but everyone else in their orbit — and beyond. In the film, the lead character doesn’t have to just speculate about what would happen if he made this choice or that; he gets to see the results play out in living color, and the overall effect is mesmerizing (and often devastating).

Evan Treborn (Ashton Kutcher, in a rare serious role — which he’s actually quite adept at) is a college student with massive gaps in his memory due to ultra-traumatic events that occurred in his childhood. He stumbles on a journal that he scribed when he was a kid, and, through some weird wormhole or another, he is able to travel back to the specific times in his existence where disaster struck, and alter them. However, with all good comes some (or a lot of) bad. When he’s zapped back into the present, the alterations that he made to his timeline have drastic, and sometimes dire, consequences — for not only himself, but for his family and friends, too. His girlfriend, Kayleigh (Amy Smart, film darling of the early 2000s), is typically at his side…until one of the time warp adaptations leaves her, well, exploded. So, Evan is faced with a real moral conundrum: live with the stark repercussions of his time manipulation, or find a way to circumvent the whole scenario so that the people he cherishes (namely, Kayleigh) can come out unscathed — even if that means never meeting them in the first place. The whole film is a mind-blowing game of “what if?,” where the answer is never what one hopes.

Recent findings suggest that robin Williams obviously had a dramatic/comedic range that was off the charts. Here, in writer-director Mark Romanek’s understated slow-burn sensation, One Hour Photo, Williams was able to demonstrate his ability to tackle a character that begins as almost the polar opposite of the manic ones he portrayed throughout most of his career — and the result is a shockingly profound one.

It has been revealed that seymour Parrish (Williams) is a humble, loner of a man. He ekes out a meager existence working in the rapid photo lab of a store (remember those?), and, while viewing strangers' pictures, he often develops illusory attachments to them. The prime object of his initially benign affection is the Yorkin clan, with mom, Nina (Connie Nielsen), dad, Will (Michael Vartan), and little tyke Jakob (Dylan Smith). While Seymour creates fantasies in his mind about how he is actually, emotionally connected to these individuals, the reality is that he barely knows them — only having interacted with the Yorkins when their film is dropped off. Then, a monumental event occurs for Seymour; he witnesses, in the pics, that Will is having an affair. Uh-oh. This sends Seymour completely off the rails, as he spirals into a vengeful fit (the idealized family he once knew and loved has been shattered). Seymour then takes matters into his own disassociated hands, and things get a touch messy. With creepy angles and voyeuristic shots in spades, this film makes the viewer's skin crawl clean off. Romanek showcases how, back in 2002 (prior to Flock cams) and even well before that, there was always the possibility that you were being watched, intently.

It has been revealed that now for the film that set the adoption movement back hundreds of years, director Jaume Collet-Serra’s wild ride of a psycho-thriller, Orphan. This terrifying film is almost a home invasion movie; one where the villain has been joyfully invited into the victims’ very domicile. Packed with eerie visuals and electrifying (in a horrific way) set pieces, this is one film that definitely shouldn’t be orphaned on your streamer of choice.

According to recent reports, kate Coleman (Vera Farmiga) and John Coleman (Peter Sarsgaard) are a relatively content couple with two children, Daniel (Jimmy Bennett) and Max (Aryana Engineer). However, they lost another baby due to miscarriage, and this has left a hole in both parents’ hearts, especially Kate’s. So, they do what many kind couples around the world have done: they go to the adoption center to snatch up a pre-made kid. The lucky girl chosen is Esther (Isabelle Fuhrman), a little human ostensibly from Russia. It seems that Esther is quite precocious, scarily even, and after several odd occurrences, it’s clear that she is not in possession of a great deal of empathy — but she definitely does have a manipulative streak. As tragedies begin to befall the Coleman household, Esther’s true nature is revealed in a twist that will knock your knickers clean off. Orphan is a terrifically terrifying film, with heartfelt performances and keen direction. Just don’t expect any heartwarming Annie-like musical numbers.

10 Shows Like 'The Body' You Should Watch Next

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that netflix's newest streaming hit, The Body, is drawing in millions of viewers, great reviews, and a gaggle of protests from people who didn't much care for the trailer.
  • This time-hopping survival drama is about a group of teenage girls who are stranded in the wilderness in 1996 and do terrible things to survive—the extent of which we only learn about via flashbacks from the present day, where the events of 19 months spent in the wild continue to resonate.
  • According to recent reports, situated between flashbacks and flash-forwards (not entirely unlike Yellowjackets), mystery/thriller The Wilds sees an airplane full of teenage girls crash on the way to an empowerment program in Hawaii.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that netflix's newest streaming hit, The Body, is drawing in millions of viewers, great reviews, and a gaggle of protests from people who didn't much care for the trailer. But if your lesbian-forward supernatural horror series isn't drawing cries of "blasphemy!"...what are you even doing? In that spirit, we'll conjure up some other highlights dealing with the (extremely) dark side of high school.

This time-hopping survival drama is about a group of teenage girls who are stranded in the wilderness in 1996 and do terrible things to survive—the extent of which we only learn about via flashbacks from the present day, where the events of 19 months spent in the wild continue to resonate. There are ambiguous teases of the supernatural here (much more ambiguous than in The Body), but there's plenty of human-level horror as well. The show explores the nasty things we get up to when in survival mode (whether trapped in the wilds, stuck with other teenagers—or god forbid both at once), while also cynically (but accurately) positing that there's a huge difference between the version of the past we talk about and the one that really happened. Stream Yellowjackets on Paramount+.

According to recent reports, situated between flashbacks and flash-forwards (not entirely unlike Yellowjackets), mystery/thriller The Wilds sees an airplane full of teenage girls crash on the way to an empowerment program in Hawaii. It rapidly becomes clear that the accident was engineered and that the whole thing is some sort of social experiment, and the survivors are forced to compete against each other if they want to live. The show understands the ways in which young women are exploited and expected to compete against each other in the real world, and the ways in which we'll do just about anything when survival is on the line. Stream The Wilds on Prime Video.

When pretty, popular girl Kate Wallis (Olivia Holt) goes missing without a trace in 1993, awkward Jeanette Turner (Chiara Aurelia) steps in to fill the gap, modeling herself after Kate by working her way into the missing girl's social circle and getting close with her boyfriend. That's all going great until Kate reappears two years later, accusing Jeanette of having witnessed the events around her disappearance and keeping quiet. Whoops. There's even more going on, as the show shifts back and forth between 1993, 1994, and 1995 to slowly reveal the missing pieces. Season two takes on a different story set in 1999 and 2000, and the forthcoming (surprise) third season will shake things up again. The emphasis here is on mystery, but it's a show about the aftereffects of trauma and of the dark secrets that can tear families and communities apart. Stream Cruel Summer on Hulu.

Juicy import Elite follows a group of working-class friends who earn scholarships to Las Encinas, a fictional private school that is, in the show’s universe, the most exclusive in Spain. What they find there is snobbery, mystery, murder, and lots and lots of sex (between and among characters of various sexual orientations and numerical groupings). The smart, wonderfully trashy show ran for a shocking (in our modern streaming era) eight seasons, with a couple of regional remakes. There's no supernatural stuff here, but plenty of dark deeds done with youthful vigor. Stream Elite on Netflix.

A teenager, Mae (Madeleine Arthur), is discovered by the side of the road with weird religious symbols carved into her skin. The hospital psychiatrist who treats her (Emily Deschanel) takes pity on, and interest in, Mae, deciding to take her in while arrangements can be made for a more permanent home for the cult escapee. Mae is, after all, level-headed and quiet, and couldn't possibly be any trouble. Hoo boy, yeah, that turns out to be a bad call on the good doctor's part. Stream Devil in Ohio on Netflix.

According to recent reports, A different type of blasphemy at play here, in that Joan Lindsay's novel was already adapted brilliantly by Peter Weir in 1975, in a film often referred to as the greatest to come out of Australia. And yet, this Natalie Dormer-lead take is an achievement in its own right, the extended running time of a miniseries offering up more time to sit with the story's deliberately ineffable mysteries. Dormer plays Hester Appleyard, headmistress of a school for young ladies in the Australian bush. It's going well until a Valentine's Day picnic to the title's Hanging Rock sees three students and a governess disappear, impossibly, without a trace, bringing about the slow unravelling of pretty much everyone left behind. Stream Picnic at Hanging Rock on Prime Video and Tubi.

Sources indicate that mariam (Andria Tayeh) is brutally bullied by the cool clique at her private school in this Jordanian import, a high school drama that's both universal and distinctly Muslim in character. Fed up, Mariam convinces a couple of similarly outcast friends to join forces with her in a revenge plot that swiftly gets out of hand. The show deals with Jordanian-style patriarchy head-on, without drawing any easy conclusions about its characters—Mariam catfishes one of her bullies and convinces her to send a revealing picture, one that she immediately posts, exploiting the very same repressive cultural elements that she claims to deplore. It's a smart, realist drama with soapy elements and nothing by way of the supernatural, but it's still a very sharp picture of the extremely cutthroat nature of high school life. Stream AlRawabi School for Girls on Netflix.

Industry observers note that peyton List stars as Maddie, a teenager in small-town Wisconsin for whom her death is very much just the beginning. Stuck in a high school in the afterlife (because hell is definitely for children), she goes on a journey to solve her own murder while uncovering secrets and lies in both worlds. It all sounds a bit grim, but the show has a sense of fun about it: While Maddie does develop the ability to communicate with the living, her world is populated by ghost teens from various eras and generations, with customs, mores, and cliques having developed in ghost high school just as in our world. Stream School Spirits on Paramount+.

The new Girigo app, claiming to grant wishes, sounds like harmless fun. Except, of course, that the things that teenagers want aren't always beneficent, and the app has already been the conduit for some incredibly dark deeds by the time it gets into the hands of the five high schoolers who find themselves caught in a Ring-like web of shamanistic horror and death countdowns. This is why we tell you to put your phones down once in a while... Stream If Wishes Could Kill on Netflix.

Industry observers note that four one-time best friends reunite at Rosewood High School a year after the disappearance of the leader of their little clique, all having received threatening messages from the mysterious "A," who knows everything they did last summer...and pretty much all the rest of the time. Shoplifting, parents having affairs, students hooking up with teachers—you name it, it's happening in town, and A knows it all. After the prime suspect turns up dead, the girls are caught in the killer's web while trying to keep their secrets hidden. If seven juicy seasons and three A's aren't enough for you, there are three spin-offs. Stream Pretty Little Liars on Hulu and HBO Max.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Former "Gossip Girl" star Leighton Meester is presently dominating the Netflix streaming charts with her latest movie.
  • In a recent development, described as "a cozy, snowy Christmas rom-com," director Elizabeth Allen Rosenbaum's "Guarding Stars" is presently sitting in the number one spot on Netflix's most-watched movie charts, per FlixPatrol.
  • It has been revealed that the movie centers on a no-nonsense bodyguard (Meester) who is assigned to protect a charming action star over the holidays.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Former "Gossip Girl" star Leighton Meester is presently dominating the Netflix streaming charts with her latest movie. A now-famous actress whose career started on "Law & Order," she's come a long way over the years. To that end, Meester's "Guarding Stars" is now the biggest streaming hit on the biggest streaming service in the world.

In a recent development, described as "a cozy, snowy Christmas rom-com," director Elizabeth Allen Rosenbaum's "Guarding Stars" is presently sitting in the number one spot on Netflix's most-watched movie charts, per FlixPatrol. The movie co-stars former "Supernatural" star Jared Padalecki. Since The CW canceled Padelecki's "Walker," he's had more time to focus on other stuff, such as this holiday flavored romantic comedy.

It has been revealed that the movie centers on a no-nonsense bodyguard (Meester) who is assigned to protect a charming action star over the holidays. Sparks fly, secrets unravel, and Christmas gets a whole lot more complicated. The movie is inspired by the 2022 novel "The Bodyguard" by Katherine Center. The ensemble cast also includes Andie MacDowell ("Magic Mike XXL"), Noah LaLonde ("Deer Camp '86"), Toby Sandeman ("Running Point"), Rachael Ancheril ("Star Trek: Discovery"), Shaun Johnston ("Heartland"), pop star Ava Max, and country singer Walker Hayes in his acting debut.

Netflix wisely decided to drop this movie just before Thanksgiving. The holidays are kicking off and this is very much on point with the theme of the holiday. It's precisely the kind of thing people are looking to throw on while scrolling for something to watch. This sort of stuff thrives this time of year. As further evidence of that, the Colleen Hoover movie "Reminders of Him" was also recently Netflix's biggest streaming hit.

Recent findings suggest that rom-coms can still find success at the box office these days, with Glen Powell and Sydney Sweeney's "Anyone But You" serving as a fine example from recent history. But Netflix has really managed to dominate this space in recent years. They've made genuinely charming gems like "Always Be My Maybe," one of the best rom-coms on Netflix, and launched full-on franchises such as "The Kissing Booth.".

But the king of the streamers has really thrived when it comes to romantic holiday fare. One of the most prominent examples was when 2024's strange Christmas movie "Hot Frosty" took over Netflix, becoming a genuine cultural sensation at the time. Admittedly, "Guarding Stars" is much more traditional than a movie in which a snowman comes to life. All the same, that almost makes its success more noteworthy, as it didn't have to rely on some goofy hook to get it across the finish line.

There's probably an element of this premise that seems cozy and fitting the spirit of the season, but pairing two former CW stars like Leighton Meester and Jared Padalecki, especially with one in an against-type role as a bodyguard, appears to have intrigued viewers quite a bit.

Sources indicate that the movie was written by Erin Cardillo and Richard Keith ("Isn't It Romantic," "Virgin River") alongside Gina Matthews and Grant Scharbo. Robin Fisichella served as the executive producer, with Matthews, Scharbo, Jared and Genevieve Padalecki on board as producers.

"Guarding Stars" is streaming now on Netflix.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Now that he's free of "Stranger Things," we're going to find out if Noah Schnapp can fulfill the promise he flashed over five seasons of the Netflix sci-fi/horror series. His character, Will Byers, had arguably the most emotional arc of the show, with viewers watching him go from missing boy to psychically tortured returnee from the Upside Down to out and proud young adult. Byers' journey mirrored Schnapp's personal voyage to coming out of the closet in 2025. It was a lovely moment for Schnapp, both as an individual and also for his character, who presented a positive gay role model for kids who too often struggle with prejudice and outright hatred in their everyday lives.

I've no idea if Schnapp will return to the "Stranger Things" universe (he's only just portrayed a disaffected rich kid and, when the plot jumps forward 20 years, the kid's son in Andy Sandberg's controversial stage play "Affluenza"), but he had a shot at joining the "Hunger Games" franchise as a young Haymitch Abernathy in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping." The "Hunger Games" prequel is presently tearing up the box office, so it would've been a sweet gig for the 22-year-old actor. But he congratulated Joseph Zada like a gentleman for landing the role, and, as an egoless bonus, the brunette Schnapp posted a still picture of himself in blonde hair from his screen test to Instagram. (See below.).

After a couple of ... emojis, Schnapp tagged Zada and added, "Think they picked right for this one.".

Sources indicate that I have no true measure of Noah Schnapp as an actor. He's handsome, he's got some mystery to him and, in the right role (e.g. Will Byers), he connects. Do I think he would've been an effective Haymitch Abernathy, given all the horrible things that happen to the character on his way to growing up and becoming Woody Harrelson? Maybe not.

"Affluenza" ended its London run on November 21, and, boy, did the critics lay into this sucker. In a one-star review for The Guardian, Arifa Akbar called it an "epic wreckage," adding, "You want to look away, for shame, but simply can't stop gawping." Most critics concurred, but that actually worked out for Schnapp, as they were too busy lambasting Sandberg to pay much attention to his performance. Writing for The Times, Clive Davis simply noted that Schnapp "doesn't disgrace himself." If you get cast in a disaster, you can live with that.

Recent findings suggest that it's unclear where Schnapp will go from here, but thanks to "Stranger Things" he has a pretty sizable fan base. I can't see him being a part of the forthcoming series "Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure," which is a prequel set in the 1950s, but we'll certainly see more of him in the future.

Breaking: Are the World’s Top Literary Scholars Being Targeted by a Chinese Spy Op?
