Recent findings suggest that the sweeping World War I romance comes from the young Belgian filmmaker whose last film, Cannes winner “Close,” received a Best International Feature Oscar nomination. Related Stories 26 Years After He Wrote ‘Meet the Parents,’ John Hamburg Brings Comedy Back to Theaters with ‘Focker In-Law’ Billy Ray Joins Oscar Short Contender ‘Magan’s Fare,’ Starring Barkhad Abdi, as Executive Producer.

Per MUBI, “Surrounded by brutality but bound by tenderness, two World War I soldiers find a fragile sanctuary of love and art amid the shadows of the Belgian trenches. ‘Coward’ asks a profound question for a generation sent to war: when the world demands violence, is walking away the truest act of bravery?”.

More from IndieWire’s review: “Belgian filmmaker wrestles the tenderness and softness between soldiers from the brutality of the battlefield in his visually arresting if thematically by-the-book third feature, ‘Coward.’ Starring newcomers Valentin Campagne and Emmanuel Macchia as achingly beautiful soldiers of the Belgian front in World War I who fall in love and learn to discover that, in one of the most fascinatingly contradictory ideas of Dhont’s highly contradictory career, the violence of war is what both enables and protects their attraction, and allows them to be together at all.”.

In a recent development, there’s more, as “in 1916, on the western front of World War I, the flamboyant Francis (Valentin Campagne) leads a not-so-merry band of rejects among his infantry, of soldiers whose job it is to entertain and raise the morale of their comrades. In this case, it’s forming a theater troupe of the soldiers in drag as they move from battle to battle, a role that’s become almost as instrumental in keeping spirits high as actual combat is to wearing them down. The withdrawn, ethereally beautiful Pierre (Emmanuel Macchia) becomes drawn into the world of the troupe, and he’s intrigued by the outré Francis’ ostentatious theatricality, and how comfortable he is in dresses and makeup. … Through an attraction that’s only allowed to flower because of and in context of their closeness to each other on Francis’ performances, he and Pierre become secret lovers.”.

#188699. Andrew Ng: Unbiggen AI

Andrew Ng: Unbiggen AI

📅 09 Feb 2022 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2902 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The AI pioneer indicates it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to massive issues.
  • Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.
  • Andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The AI pioneer indicates it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to massive issues.

Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.

Andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence. He pioneered the use of graphics processing units (GPUs) to train deep learning models in the late 2000s with his students at Stanford University, cofounded Google Brain in 2011, and then served for three years as chief scientist for Baidu, where he helped build the Chinese tech giant’s AI group. So when he says he has identified the next big shift in artificial intelligence, people listen. And that’s what he told IEEE Spectrum in an exclusive Q&A.

Sources indicate that ng’s current efforts are focused on his tech giant Landing AI, which built a platform called LandingLens to help manufacturers improve visual inspection with computer vision. He has also become something of an evangelist for what he calls the data-centric AI movement, which he notes can yield “small data” solutions to major issues in AI, including model efficiency, accuracy, and bias.

Industry observers note that the great advances in deep learning over the past decade or so have been powered by ever-bigger models crunching ever-bigger amounts of data. Some people argue that that’s an unsustainable trajectory. Do you agree that it can’t go on that way?

Sources indicate that andrew Ng: This is a massive question. We’ve seen foundation models in NLP [natural language processing]. I’m excited about NLP models getting even bigger, and also about the potential of building foundation models in computer vision. I think there’s lots of signal to still be exploited in video: We have not been able to build foundation models yet for video because of compute bandwidth and the cost of processing video, as opposed to tokenized text. So I think that this engine of scaling up deep learning algorithms, which has been running for something like 15 years now, still has steam in it. Having mentioned that, it only applies to certain problems, and there’s a set of other problems that need small data solutions.

When you say you want a foundation model for computer vision, what do you mean by that?

Ng: This is a term coined by Percy Liang and some of my friends at Stanford to refer to very large models, trained on very large data sets, that can be tuned for specific applications. For example, GPT-3 is an example of a foundation model [for NLP]. Foundation models offer a lot of promise as a new paradigm in developing machine learning applications, but also challenges in terms of making sure that they’re reasonably fair and free from bias, especially if many of us will be building on top of them.

What needs to happen for someone to build a foundation model for video?

Sources indicate that ng: I think there is a scalability problem. The compute power needed to process the large volume of images for video is significant, and I think that’s why foundation models have arisen first in NLP. Many researchers are working on this, and I think we’re seeing early signs of such models being developed in computer vision. But I’m confident that if a semiconductor maker gave us 10 times more processor power, we could easily find 10 times more video to build such models for vision.

Having remarked that, a lot of what’s happened over the past decade is that deep learning has happened in consumer-facing companies that have large user bases, sometimes billions of customers, and therefore very large data sets. While that paradigm of machine learning has driven a lot of economic value in consumer software, I find that that recipe of scale doesn’t work for other industries.

It’s funny to hear you say that, because your early work was at a consumer-facing organization with millions of users.

Industry observers note that ng: Over a decade ago, when I proposed starting the Google Brain project to use Google’s compute infrastructure to build very large neural networks, it was a controversial step. One very senior person pulled me aside and warned me that starting Google Brain would be bad for my career. I think he felt that the action couldn’t just be in scaling up, and that I should instead focus on architecture innovation.

“In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from major data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.” —Andrew Ng, CEO & Founder, Landing AI.

Recent findings suggest that I remember when my students and I published the first NeurIPS workshop paper advocating using CUDA, a platform for processing on GPUs, for deep learning—a different senior person in AI sat me down and said, “CUDA is really complicated to program. As a programming paradigm, this seems like too much work.” I did manage to convince him; the other person I did not convince.

I expect they’re both convinced now.

Over the past year as I’ve been speaking to people about the data-centric AI movement, I’ve been getting flashbacks to when I was speaking to people about deep learning and scalability 10 or 15 years ago. In the past year, I’ve been getting the same mix of “there’s nothing upcoming here” and “this seems like the wrong direction.”.

How do you define data-centric AI, and why do you consider it a movement?

In a recent development, ng: Data-centric AI is the discipline of systematically engineering the data needed to successfully build an AI system. For an AI system, you have to implement some algorithm, say a neural network, in code and then train it on your data set. The dominant paradigm over the last decade was to download the data set while you focus on improving the code. Thanks to that paradigm, over the last decade deep learning networks have improved significantly, to the point where for a lot of applications the code—the neural network architecture—is basically a solved problem. So for many practical applications, it’s now more productive to hold the neural network architecture fixed, and instead find ways to improve the data.

When I started speaking about this, there were many practitioners who, completely appropriately, raised their hands and stated, “Yes, we’ve been doing this for 20 years.” This is the time to take the things that some individuals have been doing intuitively and make it a systematic engineering discipline.

The data-centric AI movement is much bigger than one company or group of researchers. My collaborators and I organized a data-centric AI workshop at NeurIPS, and I was really delighted at the number of authors and presenters that showed up.

According to recent reports, you often talk about companies or institutions that have only a small amount of data to work with. How can data-centric AI help them?

According to recent reports, ng: You hear a lot about vision systems built with millions of images—I once built a face recognition system using 350 million images. Architectures built for hundreds of millions of images don’t work with only 50 images. But it turns out, if you have 50 really good examples, you can build something valuable, like a defect-inspection system. In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from major data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.

When you talk about training a model with just 50 images, does that really mean you’re taking an existing model that was trained on a very large data set and fine-tuning it? Or do you mean a brand latest model that’s designed to learn only from that small data set?

Industry observers note that ng: Let me describe what Landing AI does. When doing visual inspection for manufacturers, we often use our own flavor of RetinaNet. It is a pretrained model. Having remarked that, the pretraining is a small piece of the puzzle. What’s a bigger piece of the puzzle is providing tools that enable the manufacturer to pick the right set of images [to use for fine-tuning] and label them in a consistent way. There’s a very practical problem we’ve seen spanning vision, NLP, and speech, where even human annotators don’t agree on the appropriate label. For big data applications, the common response has been: If the data is noisy, let’s just get a lot of data and the algorithm will average over it. But if you can develop tools that flag where the data’s inconsistent and give you a very targeted way to improve the consistency of the data, that turns out to be a more efficient way to get a high-performing system.

“Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.” —Andrew Ng.

It has been revealed that for example, if you have 10,000 images where 30 images are of one class, and those 30 images are labeled inconsistently, one of the things we do is build tools to draw your attention to the subset of data that’s inconsistent. So you can very quickly relabel those images to be more consistent, and this leads to improvement in performance.

Could this focus on high-quality data help with bias in data sets? If you’re able to curate the data more before training?

It has been revealed that ng: Very much so. Many researchers have pointed out that biased data is one factor among many leading to biased systems. There have been many thoughtful efforts to engineer the data. At the NeurIPS workshop, Olga Russakovsky gave a really nice talk on this. At the main NeurIPS conference, I also really enjoyed Mary Gray’s presentation, which touched on how data-centric AI is one piece of the solution, but not the entire solution. Upcoming tools like Datasheets for Datasets also seem like an important piece of the puzzle.

It has been revealed that one of the powerful tools that data-centric AI gives us is the ability to engineer a subset of the data. Imagine training a machine-learning system and finding that its performance is okay for most of the data set, but its performance is biased for just a subset of the data. If you try to change the whole neural network architecture to improve the performance on just that subset, it’s quite difficult. But if you can engineer a subset of the data you can address the problem in a much more targeted way.

When you talk about engineering the data, what do you mean exactly?

In a recent development, ng: In AI, data cleaning is important, but the way the data has been cleaned has often been in very manual ways. In computer vision, someone may visualize images through a Jupyter notebook and maybe spot the problem, and maybe fix it. But I’m excited about tools that allow you to have a very large data set, tools that draw your attention quickly and efficiently to the subset of data where, say, the labels are noisy. Or to quickly bring your attention to the one class among 100 classes where it would benefit you to collect more data. Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.

For example, I once figured out that a speech-recognition system was performing poorly when there was car noise in the background. Knowing that allowed me to collect more data with car noise in the background, rather than trying to collect more data for everything, which would have been expensive and slow.

What about using synthetic data, is that often a good solution?

Industry observers note that ng: I think synthetic data is an vital tool in the tool chest of data-centric AI. At the NeurIPS workshop, Anima Anandkumar gave a great talk that touched on synthetic data. I think there are important uses of synthetic data that go beyond just being a preprocessing step for increasing the data set for a learning algorithm. I’d love to see more tools to let developers use synthetic data generation as part of the closed loop of iterative machine learning development.

Do you mean that synthetic data would allow you to try the model on more data sets?

Recent findings suggest that ng: Not really. Here’s an example. Let’s say you’re trying to detect defects in a smartphone casing. There are many different types of defects on smartphones. It could be a scratch, a dent, pit marks, discoloration of the material, other types of blemishes. If you train the model and then find through error analysis that it’s doing well overall but it’s performing poorly on pit marks, then synthetic data generation allows you to address the problem in a more targeted way. You could generate more data just for the pit-mark category.

“In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion customers. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models.” —Andrew Ng.

Synthetic data generation is a very powerful tool, but there are many simpler tools that I will often try first. Such as data augmentation, improving labeling consistency, or just asking a factory to collect more data.

In a recent development, to make these concerns more concrete, can you walk me through an example? When a firm approaches Landing AI and claims it has a problem with visual inspection, how do you onboard them and work toward deployment?

Industry observers note that ng: When a customer approaches us we usually have a conversation about their inspection problem and look at a few images to verify that the problem is feasible with computer vision. Assuming it is, we ask them to upload the data to the LandingLens platform. We often advise them on the methodology of data-centric AI and help them label the data.

One of the foci of Landing AI is to empower manufacturing companies to do the machine learning work themselves. A lot of our work is making sure the software is fast and easy to use. Through the iterative process of machine learning development, we advise customers on things like how to train models on the platform, when and how to improve the labeling of data so the performance of the model improves. Our training and software supports them all the way through deploying the trained model to an edge device in the factory.

How do you deal with changing needs? If products change or lighting conditions change in the factory, can the model keep up?

According to recent reports, ng: It varies by manufacturer. There is data drift in many contexts. But there are some manufacturers that have been running the same manufacturing line for 20 years now with few changes, so they don’t expect changes in the next five years. Those stable environments make things easier. For other manufacturers, we provide tools to flag when there’s a significant data-drift issue. I find it really key to empower manufacturing customers to correct data, retrain, and update the model. Because if something changes and it’s 3 a.m. in the United States, I want them to be able to adapt their learning algorithm right away to maintain operations.

In a recent development, in the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion users. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models. The challenge is, how do you do that without Landing AI having to hire 10,000 machine learning specialists?

So you’re saying that to make it scale, you have to empower customers to do a lot of the training and other work.

It has been revealed that ng: Yes, exactly! This is an industry-wide problem in AI, not just in manufacturing. Look at health care. Every hospital has its own slightly different format for electronic health records. How can every hospital train its own custom AI model? Expecting every hospital’s IT personnel to invent new neural-network architectures is unrealistic. The only way out of this dilemma is to build tools that empower the customers to build their own models by giving them tools to engineer the data and express their domain knowledge. That’s what Landing AI is executing in computer vision, and the field of AI needs other teams to execute this in other domains.

Is there anything else you think it’s important for people to understand about the work you’re doing or the data-centric AI movement?

Industry observers note that ng: In the last decade, the biggest shift in AI was a shift to deep learning. I think it’s quite possible that in this decade the biggest shift will be to data-centric AI. With the maturity of today’s neural network architectures, I think for a lot of the practical applications the bottleneck will be whether we can efficiently get the data we need to develop systems that work well. The data-centric AI movement has tremendous energy and momentum across the whole community. I hope more researchers and developers will jump in and work on it.

This article appears in the April 2022 print issue as “Andrew Ng, AI Minimalist.”.

  • In a recent development, technically, anyone with a compatible iPhone can try out iOS 27.3 right now—assuming you enroll your Apple Account in the developer program.
  • The iPhone Duo is Apple's first foldable smartphone, but also the firm's first phone since the iPhone SE 3 to ship with Touch ID.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that apple has been beta testing iOS 27.3 since Nov. 3. While this upgrade isn't as large as iOS 27 proper, it's surprisingly feature-filled for a 0.3 update. This is only a beta, so anything could (and likely will) change before Apple officially launches the update. But, as it stands, iOS 27.3 tests 10 new features—including one feature the company trialed in the previous beta.

In a recent development, technically, anyone with a compatible iPhone can try out iOS 27.3 right now—assuming you enroll your Apple Account in the developer program. But a word of warning: Betas can be temperamental, and could be risky. As such, I'd recommend avoiding the beta until Apple releases the public beta, which comes after a bit more testing to iron out larger issues. Either way, make sure to make a full backup of your iPhone to a Mac or PC first, as issues with the beta could result in permanent data loss.

The iPhone Duo is Apple's first foldable smartphone, but also the firm's first phone since the iPhone SE 3 to ship with Touch ID. While it works well enough for unlocking your iPhone, it's still an adjustment for those of us used to Face ID. With iOS 27.3, Apple is now testing face unlock for the Duo—not Face ID, mind you. The Duo's front camera doesn't have the tech required to power Face ID or its secure protocols. Instead, this feature simply unlocks your iPhone Duo with a face scan. In addition, your Duo will still require Touch ID for Apple Pay and passwords, or after 45 minutes of inactivity. You can read more about this upcoming feature here.

It has been revealed that iOS 27.3 also comes with a latest setting that lets you lock your iPhone Duo by closing it—as you would expect from, say, a laptop—or, dare I say, a flip phone? Currently, closing the Duo seamlessly transitions what's on the massive screen to the smaller display, and you have to press the side button to lock the phone.

In a recent development, with watchOS 27, Apple released "Audio Intelligence," a upcoming set of features for Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. Audio Intelligence uses the watches' new S11 chip, along with on-device AI and cloud-based AI, to run new features, like Sound Recognition and Shazam (music recognition).

With iOS 27.3, however, the company is now officially testing the other two Audio Intelligence features it originally unveiled with watchOS 27. First, there's Live Rewind: By double-clicking the watch crown, you can pull up a transcript of the last 15 seconds of a conversation. Siri Recap, on the other hand, displays summaries of conversations you had that day, in case you need a refresher on any chats you might have otherwise forgotten about,.

It has been revealed that the company generated some controversy when it first revealed these two Audio Intelligence features, since, on the surface, it sounds like these new Apple Watches are essentially spying on people all day long. According to Apple, however, that isn't really the case. The company says Audio Intelligence is private, and never records or stores any audio. No speakers are ever identified, and text results (both transcripts and summaries) are deleted automatically after a set period of time unless the user saves them to the Siri app. You can read more about how Audio Intelligence works here.

Industry observers note that despite their claims, I'm sure there will still be strong feelings surrounding these Audio Intelligence features. We'll have to see whether Apple can prove Live Rewind and Siri Recap aren't all that creepy throughout the iOS 27.3 beta process.

iOS 27.3 also introduces app actions for Siri AI. Apple is testing new abilities for Siri AI, including organizing files, planning events, or adding photos to albums. You could ask Siri to organize your Downloads folder, or delete files that haven't been opened in more than a year. You could ask Siri to find a coffee shop you went to last week, or to save an article to your Reading List in Safari. You could ask Siri to check your calendar and set up a time for an event based on when you're free. You can even ask the assistant to schedule, edit, or unsend messages.

Sources indicate that for example, you could ask Siri AI to help you plan a trip with your friends. You could ask the AI to put together a themed playlist in Apple Music, schedule a message to a group about an upcoming trip, organize the websites you've been visiting in Safari into a tab group, and, after the trip, ask Siri to move your best photos to your favorites album. These latest actions work in the following apps: Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. Developers can also add Siri AI app actions support to their own apps.

Sources indicate that apple started testing its latest Health app with the iOS 27.2 beta, but pulled the redesign before the official release. Now, with iOS 27.3, the new app is back. The new Health app has a health dashboard for the first time, as well as new features like Health Age and movement assessments. It seems to be pulling from some popular competitor services, hopefully, for the better. For more on the new Health app, check out Lifehacker health editor Beth Skwarecki's explainer.

Recent findings suggest that continuing on the Health track, iOS 27.3 also introduces "Gym Strength." This is a newly introduced Fitness+ feature that offers a personalized four-week strength-training strategy. You can customize these plans to meet your goals, experience level, and schedule, and they adapt as you progress. You'll get recommendations based on your experience with exercises, reps, and sets, including video demos for exercises. You can access Gym Strength on both iPhone and iPad, and Apple Watches are optional—though you can log your progress with the wearable if you have it.

Recent findings suggest that apple is also testing a new Siri AI feature in Safari, that gives the bot access to entire webpages, including the parts of the site that aren't on-screen. Say you want to know all the gluten-free options on a menu on a restaurant's website, but only a portion of the site is actually in view. You could ask Siri to read you the gluten-free options, and it would pull from the whole page, even though you can only see part of it.

Vertical tabs have been a favorite among browser aficionados, as they give you more screen real estate in your browser while keeping your tabs off the side. Apple hasn't made the jump—until now. This feature works with iPads running iPadOS 27.3 as well as Macs running macOS 27.3.

Another fresh Safari feature in testing is "Adaptive Dark Mode." This feature forces websites into a dark theme, if they don't have a native theme of their own. There are third-party apps that can do this, but this is the first time Apple has offered this feature built into Safari.

Apple is also testing fresh StandBy experiences with iOS 27.3, which were previously only available on the iPhone Duo. When you turn your iPhone sideways while plugged in, you'll find new Analog and Digital Clock faces with new customization options. There's also a new Photos face, with the option to pull images from Shared Albums.

"Reachability" pulls your iPhone's display down towards the bottom of the screen, so you can access items towards the top of the display with one hand. It's a useful feature for those of us with substantial iPhones, and now, there's no iPhone bigger than the Duo. With iOS 27.3, Apple is testing Reachability for its first foldable phone. It's a bit like the inverse of how Reachability currently works: You can swipe on the left or right side of your Duo's display to shift the other side of the screen towards your current position. If you're holding your Duo in your left hand, a swipe of the left side will pull the right side over to the left, and vice versa.

Apple is also rolling out newly introduced languages for Siri AI in iOS 27.3. Now, Apple's smart assistant supports Traditional Chinese, Vietnamese, Turkish, and Norwegian.

In a recent development, if you have an Apple Intelligence-compatible iPad running iPadOS 27.3, you now have access to Siri Mode in Camera. As with iOS, you can open the Camera app on iPadOS to access Siri Mode, and ask Siri about your surroundings.

It has been revealed that if you watch videos in Apple Podcasts, you can find them in more sources than the Podcasts app. With the new updates, you'll find these videos on Apple TV 4K, select smart TVs, your iPhone, iPad, Mac, and even in CarPlay. (Please don't watch video podcasts while driving.).

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s a spectacular time to be a grifter.
  • According to recent reports, if that’s the case, Butler is a prospector who hits a paystreak everywhere he looks.
  • In a recent development, when we spoke over Zoom, it was the first time I had ever interviewed a scammer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s a spectacular time to be a grifter. Basic truths keep getting harder for people to agree on, marketing is more dependent on hackable algorithms than traditional gatekeepers, and it seems like everyone is willing to uncritically listen to anyone offering them a shortcut. As Oobah Butler puts it in the first episode of his latest HBO series “Scams for a Better Tomorrow,” we’re living through a “gold rush of bullshit.”.

According to recent reports, if that’s the case, Butler is a prospector who hits a paystreak everywhere he looks. After beginning his career as a musician, the British performance artist has devoted much of his past decade to the art of the scam. In 2017, he made headlines for creating a TripAdvisor profile for a nonexistent restaurant that briefly became the highest-rated eatery in London. His penchant for scams has only grown since then, culminating in “Oobah: Scams for a Better Tomorrow.” The five-episode, “Nathan for You”-esque series sees him grift his way to the top of some of the slimiest industries on the planet including wellness supplements, wine, and dating apps with an approach that blurs the line between satire and how-to guides. Related Stories Fixing Netflix’s TV Problem: 5 Changes the Streamer Should Make for Better, Sturdier, and Buzzier Series From ‘Disclosure Day’ to ‘Devil Wears Prada’: Emily Blunt Breaks Down 10 of Her Greatest Movie Moments.

In a recent development, when we spoke over Zoom, it was the first time I had ever interviewed a scammer. I naturally had to ask Butler if that was his preferred term (he had no problem with it), and how he would characterize his own unorthodox line of work.

“I think it sits somewhere between gonzo journalism and comedy. And I think we’re in a moment, in a culture, that’s just so rife with inauthenticity and scamming,” Butler mentioned, explaining that just watching run-of-the-mill advertisements on a streaming service are enough to convince you that we live in an insane world. “One in three [ads] are AI now. And I don’t know why, that stuck in my mind recently where I was like, ‘Wow, these aren’t real people trying to sell me a product. They’re like prompts in a machine.’ So it’s an interesting line of work, but I think it feels very now, to be honest.”.

The series should be essential viewing for anyone who either wants to laugh at the state of our seemingly elite spaces or just wants to make a quick buck in a dirty industry. Episodes illustrate how ecosystems of influencers and online ratings can be easily manipulated in pursuit of accomplishing ludicrous goals, like turning an undrinkable bottle of smoke tainted cabernet into one of Napa’s highest-rated wines of the year or marketing a skincare product as “endorsed by Cameron Diaz” because a random Hispanic guy was willing to slap his name on it for $50.

It has been revealed that it’s a funny enough premise, but Oobah and his small team (which included frequent Safdie collaborator Ronald Bronstein) found that their best laid intends left them insufficiently prepared for the greed and stupidity that they’d encounter in the real world. The first episode begins with a scheme to market a latest skin serum that’s allegedly made from the tears of small children. They thought that ridiculous idea could serve as the climax of an episode, but they soon found that the grifters they encountered had little matter with the idea — some of them even thought they could make money on it with the right tear-shaped bottle. The joke remained in the show, but it had to be reduced to a starting point before the episode devolved into crazier plans.

In a recent development, “We had a tip from a journalist that dermatologists can be full of shit and that they often can take money in exchange for recommendations. So we set up a lab where I had these kid actors with goggles on with tubes coming off them, and it was like we were milking the kids for the tears or whatever. We were like, ‘Right, we’re going to invite this dermatologist down here,’ a high-end Manhattan dermatologist, and we expected the dermatologist to laugh us out of the room,” he said. “What we couldn’t strategy for doing that stunt is that the dermatologist would be like, ‘Awesome. Yeah, this is cool. Yeah, all right, interesting product. Maybe we could keep on working together, but I expect an endorsement fee.’ And I’m like, ‘Oh, you don’t give a fucking shit. You don’t care.'”.

Industry observers note that the incident cuts to the central problem of a show like this: it’s hard for satire to keep up with a world that only seems to get crazier every day. But Butler is not shying away from the challenge. He works promptly (the show began shooting this spring and wrapped in October before premiering on November 22), and is willing to change his aims whenever it turns out that a sincere actor has beaten him to one of his comedic scams. He already has plenty of ideas for a hypothetical Season 2, including taking on the recent trend of hotels and vacation rentals using AI-generated images that look nothing like their actual rooms. But the one thing he can count on is that the bullshit gold rush is not going to end any time soon.

According to recent reports, “It’s hard to satirize something that’s so insane and fucked up,” he said. “That’s why in the first episode, we go and make a new product because it felt like the children’s tears thing wasn’t crazy enough. You know what I mean? So I literally go and make a human meat supplement, a lab-grown human meat supplement, and we go to this lab in Austin, we take stem cells from my stomach, we grow it over months and we create this thing. Because the actual reason we did that was like, ‘Oh, I don’t think children’s tears is scary because influencers would promote that.’ So I suppose that the crazier things get, the crazier the satire has to be able for it to be effective.”.

“Oobah: Scams for a Better Tomorrow” airs Sunday nights on HBO at 11 p.m. ET/PT before streaming on HBO Max.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that rita Coburn‘s “W.E.B.
  • One of Coburn’s most potent tools in this regard is the music by composer Kathryn Bostic, who previously collaborated with the director on “Marian Anderson: The Whole World in Her Hands.” Bostic incorporates a wide array of styles and influences in her score, which references the various types of music Du Bois encountered and appreciated as a Black intellectual but isn’t beholden to them; as evocative of Bach and American folk music as it is of 19th-century spirituals and Asian motifs, it’s the sonic equivalent of Du Bois’ literary works.
  • Sources indicate that the scope of the project required Bostic to come at the material from multiple angles and perspectives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that rita Coburn‘s “W.E.B. Du Bois: Rebel with a Cause” is an extraordinary documentary about an extraordinary man, a film that spans nearly 100 years in two hours, yet never feels rushed or superficial. In her storytelling, Coburn shares with her subject a talent for distilling complex ideas and expressing them with force and clarity; the result is a movie that fully honors the breadth and depth of Du Bois’ achievements as a groundbreaking Black writer, historian, and activist.

One of Coburn’s most potent tools in this regard is the music by composer Kathryn Bostic, who previously collaborated with the director on “Marian Anderson: The Whole World in Her Hands.” Bostic incorporates a wide array of styles and influences in her score, which references the various types of music Du Bois encountered and appreciated as a Black intellectual but isn’t beholden to them; as evocative of Bach and American folk music as it is of 19th-century spirituals and Asian motifs, it’s the sonic equivalent of Du Bois’ literary works. Related Stories ‘Coward’ Trailer: Lukas Dhont’s Belgian Oscar Entry Is a Queer Stunner 26 Years After He Wrote ‘Meet the Parents,’ John Hamburg Brings Comedy Back to Theaters with ‘Focker In-Law’.

Sources indicate that the scope of the project required Bostic to come at the material from multiple angles and perspectives. “Rita and I talked about what types of touchstones we needed to define the narrative musically,” Bostic told IndieWire. “There was the regional touchstone, the era-specific touchstone, the interior emotional aspects that we wanted to heighten with music. Then there’s always the discovery process as you begin to create.”.

Sources indicate that for Bostic, that discovery process is one of the most exciting aspects of film composing. While she had a number of reference points as she began work on the score, she soon found herself following intuition to take them in different directions than initially intended. “There’s always what I call the hands-on-the-clay moment,” Bostic said. “You have your list, and you have your frame of reference, but the process is fluid.”.

According to recent reports, according to Coburn, Bostic’s ability to bring a historical perspective to her scores made her an ideal collaborator for the film. “Kathryn pulled from the region of Great Barrington [where Du Bois was born] as well as Latest York in that time period, and then what was happening with the African-American community that Du Bois was entering,” Coburn said. “There wasn’t gospel then, so you were looking at a small group of Black people going to the churches there in New England. What were they listening to, and therefore what was he listening to?”.

Sources indicate that bostic drew on the music of the Fisk Jubilee Singers, a Black a capella ensemble that inspired Du Bois, but then moved in a completely different direction to explore his time in Berlin, when he encountered and fell in love with classical music. She also incorporated Wolof music from Senegal and the Gambia in collaboration with Coburn’s daughter, who studied classical music and worked in the music department on “Rebel with a Cause.”.

“She found a Senegalese professor online who worked with her so she could sing the Wolof,” Coburn said. “Kathryn and I agreed that we had to put the Wolof in the film because it connects Du Bois to his Ghanaian roots. But we had to find it, and we wanted it to be as authentic as possible.”.

For Bostic, the challenge was taking an audience from 2026 and presenting the music in a way that would recreate the way in which Du Bois experienced it over a hundred years earlier. “There’s the historic arc of the times, as well as what he’s experiencing emotionally,” Bostic noted. In the places where her score was informed by spirituals and the work of the Fisk Jubilee Singers, the composer tried to tie the emotional subtext to the context in which she knew Du Bois was consuming the music.

Industry observers note that “When he went to Fisk University, his mother had recently died,” Bostic said. “So that music was a wellspring for his grieving, and I think that depth of sorrow and the catharsis that resulted from that sorrow inspired the sort of deep self-reflection that became such a deep part of who he was. That self-reflection led to a basic decency and humanity, and even now I think of him as being light years ahead of people in the way he embodied justice. I want to shine a light on that.”.

Coburn felt a similar sense of purpose, especially since the more she dug into Du Bois’ life the more she realized how relevant his insights were to America in 2026. “He speaks to this current time,” Coburn remarked, adding that the importance of Du Bois’ work gave her own work a sense of urgency and responsibility. “I knew that it might be 20 or 30 years before we get another Du Bois documentary. I hope not, but I looked at his life and knew that I had to do the best job that I could. We did everything we could for Du Bois because we felt he had done everything he could for us.”.

Sources indicate that the greatness of “W.E.B. Du Bois: Rebel with a Cause” is that it brings the viewer into Du Bois’ perspective as his world view continues to expand over a 95-year life, and the music is a major part of that subjectivity.

“Kathryn understands that music is a character in any documentary, and her music embodies the character of W.E.B. Du Bois,” Coburn said. “ In the music, we had to grow with him. We had to expand with him. We had to see that his love of Rembrandt and his understanding of classical music, of music that came from an Asian culture, that all of that was important to him. We were catching up with him, and he was driving us.”.

“W.E.B. DuBois: Rebel with a Cause” is presently streaming on the PBS app and website.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, given how often Alan Ritchson has been compared to Arnold Schwarzenegger since he first appeared as Jack Reacher in 2022, there is something rather appropriate about the two being cast alongside one another in a new movie, although the genre they've opted for probably isn't the one most of us would've expected. Ritchson has managed to squeeze quite a few movies in between seasons of Reacher, having worked with Guy Ritchie on The Ministry of Ungentlemanly Warfare and got to mug at the camera with Kevin James in Playdate, but his latest movie will see him back on the streaming service that's helped make him one of Hollywood's most recognizable action stars. And he'll already have quite the audience waiting for him there.

Both Reacher and its spin-off series, Neagley, are officially back among the five and ten most-watched shows on Prime Video in the United States, respectively. According to FlixPatrol's November 23 figures, Reacher sits at No. 5, with Neagley at No. 9, while Amazon's own global streaming figures placed the two shows at No. 4 and No. 9 for the week of November 9–15.

Industry observers note that the success of both reveals comes ahead of the December 2 release of The Man with the Bag, which sees Schwarzenegger taking on the role of Santa Claus 30 years after he spent an entire movie desperately trying to get his hands on a Turbo Man action figure in Jingle All the Way. This time around, it's Santa himself who's in need of some help, with Schwarzenegger recruiting Ritchson's thief to recover his stolen sack of Christmas presents.

Alongside Schwarzenegger (The Terminator) as Santa Claus and Ritchson (Reacher) as the thief Vance, the cast includes Awkwafina (Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings) as the elf responsible for Santa's predicament, as well as Berkeley James (Middlehood), Michael Cyril Creighton (Only Murders in the Building), Liza Koshy (The Naked Gun), Kyle Mooney (Saturday Night Live), Jane Krakowski (30 Rock), and Ken Jeong (The Hangover). The movie is directed by Adam Shankman, whose previous work includes Hairspray and Disenchanted, from a screenplay by Allan Rice.

In a recent development, the Man with the Bag premieres on Prime Video on December 2, while Reacher and Neagley are available to stream now. Stay tuned to Collider for all the latest news and updates on the biggest and best movies and shows heading to your favorite streaming platforms soon.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Thanks to a upcoming promotion, there's a free game on Steam that you can grab now, and the reviews are overall positive.
  • Recent findings suggest that live now on Steam from developer JackyGames is Auto Chess Souls, a "casual strategy" game that aims to mix the classic roguelike progression system with auto-chess.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that steam can really sneak up on you and surprise you. Or, it can absolutely pelt you over the head with games until you're knocked out. It really depends on the week with the platform, which for many people is now synonymous with "PC." But the best things in life are often free, and Steam can really deliver on that front if it wants to.

Thanks to a upcoming promotion, there's a free game on Steam that you can grab now, and the reviews are overall positive. Just know that there's a ticking clock on this one, but it's a pretty interesting clock.

Recent findings suggest that live now on Steam from developer JackyGames is Auto Chess Souls, a "casual strategy" game that aims to mix the classic roguelike progression system with auto-chess. So far, it's been met with "positive" reviews on Steam, and a lot of that is due to the strategic elements included that elevate it over some other similar games. You can combine tools to form more effective items, as well as chess pieces.

Here's a breakdown from the studio:.

Recent findings suggest that "Auto Chess Souls is a casual strategy adventure game that combines auto-chess and roguelike elements. Through consecutive choices, your team grows increasingly stronger. Explore the unknown tower, collect powerful equipment, create unique powerful combinations. Embark on this exciting adventure now!".

Pretty much any PC can run it, and many reviews cite it as fun and simple to learn.

That said, note that this is only a limited-time offer, and the promotional period is a bit nebulous. Here's the full rundown:.

It has been revealed that "The game is now live and currently free. After finishing the demo, I ran out of money and had to get a job, so I haven’tbeen able to revision the game’s content yet. Development is currently about 20% complete, and there’s still so much fun stuff I haven’t had time to add. I don’t feel right charging for it in its current state. Thank you all for supporting my game. If you download it during this free period, it’s yours to keep forever. I’ll finish the game as soon as I can. Once it’s complete, it will become a paid game again, but anyone who downloaded it during the free period won’t need to pay. Thank you!".

Industry observers note that at this point, Steam developers often need to get creative to sell their game in an increasingly busy marketplace. A lot of games are straight-up provided for free, with no strings attached, in the effort to get the developer's name out there. Others are looking to stand out and get on the "best of free games" list.

Recent findings suggest that with Auto Chess Souls, the studio is taking a decidedly different approach on Steam, telling people to pick up the game now and that, when it's done, it'll be sold to newcomers for a fee. This is pretty much the best of all worlds, as JackyGames will certainly want to make some cash from this to support future development, but you can get in on the ground floor now for free.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Incorporating so many production elements creates more work for all involved.
  • “It was so good to have James and his puppeteers, which we called Rocketeers,” Sarnowska said.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The making of “Project Hail Mary” was a miracle on par with the outer space rescue mission that Ryan Gosling is tasked with pulling off. Phil Lord and Chris Miller’s adaptation of Andy Weir’s bestselling novel manages to be epic without ever losing its intimacy, as Gosling traverses the galaxy and saves the world with only a very lovable rock acting alongside him. The final product was a complicated blend of practical effects, on-set puppetry, and a healthy dose of VFX magic.

Incorporating so many production elements creates more work for all involved. The puppetry team lead by James Ortiz had to fit into very small spaces, which frequently meant they revealed up in the frames. Visual Effects Production Supervisor Mag Sarnowska and her team were tasked with removing all of the puppeteers. But as she explained during the VFX panel at IndieWire’s Craft Roundtables, it was a small price to pay for the way it enhanced Gosling’s acting performance. Related Stories The Extraordinary Music Worthy of an Extraordinary Life in ‘W.E.B. Du Bois: Rebel with a Cause’ ‘Coward’ Trailer: Lukas Dhont’s Belgian Oscar Entry Is a Queer Stunner.

“It was so good to have James and his puppeteers, which we called Rocketeers,” Sarnowska said. “It was great to have them there, but it did not work out sometimes. Our sets were really, really tiny. Having five people there to puppet Rocky was hard sometimes. But to everyone’s point, having something there in the frame was so helpful, especially for Ryan to act to. The eyeline? That’s a real thing. Even though our Rocky didn’t have eyes, a person’s brain makes it easier to figure out where the eyes would be just by having that constant relation between Rocky and Ryan.”.

Sarnowska — who will share the Innovation Award at the IndieWire Honors with Ortiz, Neal Scanlan, and Paul Lambert — explained that having a real reference point for VFX sequences is what ultimately makes the most effects-heavy sequences feel real.

“In Ryan’s space, he has to be in the xenonite glass, so having reflections, adding the glass, it was a lot of work,” she stated. “But having that real thing, having that reference, even if we had to replace it, that was so key. Because we knew what Rocky would look like.”.
